title: Don't be turned into a Caesar
hook: beware of becoming an emperor inside; stay simple, kind, unaffected (Meditations 6.30)

segments.voice: Yesterday, outward show: Marcus called his purple robe sheep's wool dyed in shellfish blood. Metal, glass and a loan.

Day two hundred. A coworker got promoted, and changed, a little at a time. They started saying we at the leadership level. They stopped eating lunch with the old team. Their jokes got less funny and everyone laughed harder. It can happen to anyone with a little power: the team lead, the head of the committee, the person with a few thousand followers. Marcus had the throne itself. And he watched himself for exactly this.
screen: `DAY TWO HUNDRED.` → `A LITTLE AT A TIME.` → `DON'T BE TURNED INTO A CAESAR.`

segments.voice: Here's how Book Six, section thirty, begins in George Long's translation: "Take care that thou art not made into a Cæsar, that thou art not dyed with this dye." Then three small words: for such things happen. Remember the dye from a week ago? The soul is dyed by the thoughts. Here Marcus fears one particular color, the color of being emperor, soaking in until it's all the way through. In the Greek, some readers think he made up a word for it, something like: don't get Caesared. Being called Caesar was his job. He's afraid of Caesar becoming who he is. The cure is a list for himself: stay simple, good, pure, serious, free from showing off, a friend of justice, reverent toward the gods, kind, affectionate, and strong in doing what's right. Then he holds up the man who raised him to the throne, his adoptive father, the emperor Antoninus Pius: how steady he was, how gentle, how little he cared for empty fame, how carefully he listened, how he never rushed a decision, content with plain food and a plain bed. Be his pupil still, Marcus tells himself. Life is short. There is only one fruit of this life, he says: a reverent disposition and acts for the common good. You probably aren't about to be made an emperor. But everyone gets some little throne: a title, a role, a bit of being needed. The question is whether it stays a job or becomes a costume you can't take off. Your line: stay simple.
screen: `TAKE CARE: NOT MADE INTO A CAESAR.` · `A LIST: SIMPLE, GOOD, KIND.` · `REMEMBER ANTONINUS.` · then, large: `STAY SIMPLE.`

segments.voice: Notice which little throne you sit on: a title, being the one who knows, the busy one, the one people come to. Imagine setting it on the floor for these two minutes. Underneath it is just a person breathing; rest as that person.
Caesared. Marcus's rare word for being turned into a Caesar, letting the role dye him through instead of staying simple, good and kind. Today's word.
Your line: stay simple. A title is a job, not who you are. Two hundred days in, and thank you for every one.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use this passage as a check on their own roles and titles, and many traditions have practices of humility for people in positions of power.

original.note: Greek: from Marcus's warning 'don't be Caesared', a rare word; some readers think Marcus coined it.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't become a tyrant.
what it means: don't let your role soak into you until it's who you are.
what a scholar hears: a rare word, perhaps Marcus's own coinage, apokaisarōthēs, 'be un-made into a Caesar', beside baphēs, 'be dyed', echoing the dye image of 5.16.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: hook no longer opens with uplift ('Look how far you've walked') and 'think of'; superlatives ('all the power there was', 'the most powerful man in the world') removed; the coinage claim is now 'some readers think'; myth item about the coinage replaced; 'one fruit' line paraphrased closer to Long ('a pious disposition and social acts').
Confirm the Long 1862 wording exactly: 'Take care that thou art not made into a Cæsar, that thou art not dyed with this dye; for such things happen.'
Greek 'μὴ ἀποκαισαρωθῇς, μὴ βαφῇς': confirm spelling and accents, and the claim that it appears to be a coinage (commentators generally say so).

The list is paraphrased from Long ('simple, good, pure, serious, free from affectation, a friend of justice, a worshipper of the gods, kind, affectionate, strenuous in all proper acts'). 'Reverent toward the gods' renders 'worshipper of the gods'. Confirm.
Antoninus portrait details (plain food, plain bed, careful listening, no rushing) are paraphrased from 6.30 and 1.16; confirm which are in 6.30.
'The only fruit of this life is a good character and acts that help others' paraphrases 6.30's 'there is only one fruit of this terrene life...'. Confirm.
